claims.text: Conventional strengthening of structural metals and alloys often increases strength at the expense of tensile ductility.
Grain refinement and precipitation hardening are examples of treatments that typically produce high strength at the expense of ductility.
A machine-learning model trained on processing and mechanical-property databases can predict and optimize heat-treatment and deformation cycles.
Machine-learning optimization can identify non-intuitive processing cycles that overcome the strength-ductility trade-off.
The optimized processing cycles will refine alloy grain size.
The optimized processing cycles will produce fine, coherent nanoprecipitates.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces relieve stress concentrations that could otherwise initiate premature cracking.
Engineered grain boundaries facilitate dislocation motion without early failure.
Solid-solution strengthening acts synergistically with coherent precipitate formation to enhance both strength and ductility.
A coherent-nanoprecipitation strategy can produce simultaneous ultrahigh strength and substantial tensile ductility at ambient temperature.
The machine-learning-optimized alloy will improve both strength and ductility relative to a conventionally processed counterpart.
The proposed approach is primarily applicable to structural alloy systems having extensive processing and mechanical-property data.
Performance gains from the proposed approach may depend on data quality and the alloy system.
The predictive precision of the machine-learning model and the scalability of its processing window across alloy chemistries remain unestablished.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in both strength and ductility over a conventionally processed control would falsify the hypothesis.
